subindicator_definition: The Area Time Equivalent Ratio (ATER) is a measure of the productivity of an intercropping system. It is calculated by dividing the total yield of the intercrop by the yield of a sole crop grown for the same duration. The ATER is calculated as follows: ATER = (Total yield of intercrop) / (Yield of sole crop grown for the same duration). The ATER is particularly useful in intercropping systems where the crops have different growth durations. For example, if a farmer intercrops a fast-growing crop with a slow-growing crop, the faster-growing crop will produce a yield before the slower-growing crop. The ATER will take into account the different growth durations of the crops and will give a more accurate measure of the overall productivity of the intercropping system.

subindicator_definition: Community-weighted mean (CWM) of a functional trait, calculated as the average trait value across species in a community weighted by each species' relative abundance. Captures the dominant functional expression of a community.
subindicator_details: Calculated as CWM = Σ(pi · ti), where pi = relative abundance of species i and ti = trait value of species i. Units depend on the trait being weighted (e.g., g for seed mass, m for plant height).

subindicator_definition: Represents the number of equally abundant species that would produce the same diversity value.

notes: NA

subindicator_definition: Fisher's alpha (α), a parametric diversity index based on the log-series distribution of species abundances. Relatively independent of sample size and widely used in tropical community ecology.
subindicator_details: Calculated by solving S = α·ln(1 + N/α), where S = number of species and N = number of individuals. Higher α indicates greater diversity.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: Margalef's diversity index (d), which standardises observed species richness by the logarithm of total abundance. Intended to account for the effect of sample size on richness comparisons.
subindicator_details: Calculated as d = (S - 1) / ln(N), where S = observed species count and N = total number of individuals. Higher values indicate greater diversity per unit of sampled abundance.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: The Shannon index of diversity. Synonym for the Shannon-Wiener Index (subindicator code 350).

notes: NA

subindicator_definition: The Shannon-Wiener (or Shannon-Weaver) diversity index (H'), an information-theoretic measure combining species richness and evenness. Higher values indicate greater diversity.
subindicator_details: Calculated as H' = -Σ(pi · ln(pi)), where pi = relative abundance of species i. Typically bounded between 0 and ~5 in natural communities; sensitive to both richness and evenness.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: Generic Simpson index of diversity. Ambiguous naming: may refer to Simpson's D (dominance), 1-D (diversity), or 1/D (reciprocal). When reported without qualification, this row is used; for precise formulations see codes 326 (1/D) and 327 (1-D).
subindicator_details: Authors often report 'Simpson Index' without specifying the formulation. Extractors should check context (values near 1 = likely 1-D; values up to ~10+ = likely 1/D; values near 0 = likely D).
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: Simpson's dominance index calculated as (1 - D), where D is the sum of squared proportional abundances. Measures the probability that two randomly selected individuals belong to different species.
subindicator_details: Calculated as 1 - D where D = sum(pi^2). Ranges from 0 (single species) to approaching 1 (high diversity). A non-linear transformation related to Simpson's reciprocal (Hill number q=2).
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: measuring the effective number of species weighted by dominance. Higher values indicate greater diversity and lower dominance by any single species.
subindicator_details: Calculated as 1/D where D = sum of squared proportional abundances.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: Diversity measured at taxonomic levels above species, such as genus or family richness. Captures broader phylogenetic representation in a community
subindicator_details: Useful when species-level identification is not possible or when higher-level diversity patterns are of interest.

subindicator_definition: The integrated area under a curve of disease severity plotted against time. Summarises the cumulative disease pressure over a growing season or epidemic period.
subindicator_details: Calculated as AUDPC = Σ[(yi + yi+1)/2 · (ti+1 − ti)], where yi = disease severity at time ti. Higher AUDPC indicates greater cumulative disease damage.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: The rate of CO2 efflux from the soil surface, reflecting the metabolic activity of soil organisms and root respiration. Used as a proxy for overall soil biological activity.

subindicator_definition: Pielou's evenness index (J'), a measure of how evenly individuals are distributed among species in a community, independent of species richness. Values range from 0 (one species dominates) to 1 (all species equally abundant). Examples include: Pielou's evenness index (J'), equitability index.
subindicator_details: Calculated as J' = H'/ln(S) where H' = Shannon index and S = species richness. A pure evenness measure decoupled from richness (Pielou 1966). Chao & Ricotta (2019) provide a modern evenness framework linked to Hill numbers.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: An evenness measure derived from the Shannon index, expressing how close observed Shannon diversity is to the maximum possible for a given number of species. Equivalent to Pielou's J'.
subindicator_details: Calculated as E = H' / ln(S), where H' = Shannon index and S = species richness. Ranges from 0 (complete dominance) to 1 (perfect evenness).
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: A general measure of how evenly individuals are distributed among the species in a community, independent of total richness. Distinct from Pielou's J' in that it can refer to any evenness formulation (e.g., E1/D, Heip's evenness, Shannon evenness).
subindicator_details: Various formulations exist; most are bounded approximately 0-1. Low values indicate dominance by a few species; high values indicate equitable distribution.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: The total mass of living microbial organisms in the soil, typically measured as microbial biomass carbon (MBC). Reflects the size of the soil microbial community
subindicator_details: Usually measured by chloroform fumigation-extraction method.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: The observed number of distinct species (or morphospecies) recorded in a defined area or sample. The most intuitive measure of biodiversity, but sensitive to sampling effort.
subindicator_details: Raw count of species. For comparisons across sites with unequal sampling effort, rarefied or estimated richness (e.g., Chao1, Jackknife) should be used instead.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: A non-parametric species richness estimator that uses the proportion of samples containing each species to estimate total richness.
subindicator_details: Bootstrap = Sobs + sum(1 - pi)^n where pi = proportion of samples containing species i, n = number of samples.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: An abundance-based non-parametric estimator of species richness that accounts for undetected species using the frequency of rare species (singletons and doubletons) in a sample.
subindicator_details: Chao1 = Sobs + (f1^2 / 2*f2) where Sobs = observed species, f1 = singletons, f2 = doubletons.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: An incidence-based non-parametric estimator of species richness using presence/absence data across multiple samples. Accounts for undetected species based on the frequency of unique and duplicate detections.
subindicator_details: Chao2 = Sobs + (q1^2 / 2*q2) where q1 = uniques, q2 = duplicates across samples.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: A non-parametric estimator of total species richness that corrects the observed count using the number of species found in only one sample (uniques) or one/two individuals (singletons/doubletons).
subindicator_details: First-order: Jack1 = Sobs + q1·(n-1)/n, where q1 = uniques and n = number of samples. Second-order jackknife incorporates doubletons. Reduces underestimation bias in incompletely sampled communities.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: Species richness estimated by rarefaction: the expected number of species that would be observed if all samples were standardised to the same (smaller) sampling effort or abundance. Removes the confounding effect of unequal sampling.
subindicator_details: Calculated using the Hurlbert/Sanders rarefaction formula. Enables fair comparisons of richness across sites with different sample sizes. Distinct from extrapolation-based estimators like Chao1.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: Berger-Parker dominance (d) is one of the simplest diversity/dominance indices used in community ecology. It's defined as: d = N_max / N_total Where: N_max = the number of individuals (or abundance) of the single most abundant species in the sample N_total = the total number of individuals across all species in the sample So it's just the proportional abundance of the single dominant (most common) species in the community.
notes: NA

subindicator_definition: Jaccard's coefficient of community similarity, a beta-diversity metric that quantifies the proportion of shared species between two communities relative to the total number of unique species across both.
subindicator_details: Calculated as J = a / (a + b + c), where a = shared species, b = species unique to community 1, c = species unique to community 2. Ranges from 0 (no shared species) to 1 (identical composition).
notes: NA
